links.summary: Subframe is a macOS design tool where "the canvas is based on HTML & React, so you can implement it exactly as designed" — drag & drop, layers and inspector, plus built-in browser tabs and Claude Code and Codex connected directly inside: "It's a browser, for building." Free is $0/month for one project with unlimited viewers & editors and your own Claude / Codex subscription (limited AI credits); Pro is $20/editor/month for unlimited projects and 6x AI credits.

Koboyo is an infinite canvas where you "Pick a tool from here" and "Double-click anywhere to add text or pick a tool" — rectangle (R), ellipse (O), arrow (A), plus Slides & Diagrams as Code, zoom & reset view, and keyboard shortcuts. It keeps the instructions on the canvas itself: "Double-click anywhere to add text or pick a tool."

Complexity is never a conscious design goal, but "technologies are added, but are rarely removed," so stacks become sprawling patchworks where more parts means more cognitive complexity, more failure candidates, and engineers who are jacks of all trades but masters of none. The answer is Buckminster Fuller's ephemeralization — "do more and more with less and less until eventually you can do everything with nothing" — which at Heroku meant folding its special-snowflake core database into Heroku Postgres, retiring products like `ssl:ip`, moving non-ephemeral data out of Redis, and feeding dead components to a burn party. Practice it by retiring old technology, standardizing on one database and one runtime, not adopting new tools the day (or year) they ship, avoiding custom technology and NIH, and using services rather than operating software yourself.

Tripwire calls itself "the firewall for your OSS projects": install the GitHub App and it starts ingesting contributor activity — change requests, comments, and the rest — so every event runs through your workflows where triggers fire, rules evaluate, and actions decide. Rules like account age, rate limits, hidden links and max files changed are composable, org members are exempt, runs are public while deciding stays gated, and a blocked change request gets "One comment. One check. Zero noise." It's not launched yet — the page asks you to request access, join the beta, get early access to rules, or claim your spot on the waitlist.

dither-kit is dithered charts & components for shadcn/ui: install via `@dither-kit/cli` — "lockfile for update / diff, pulls core + deps automatically" — or paste into Claude Code, Cursor, or any agent to install + wire up a chart, with files landing in components/dither-kit/. It ships area, bar, line, pie and radar charts plus standalone button and gradient components, tweakable through knobs like variant, bloom, stackType, colors, animate and interactive, and a floating dial panel. No pricing or license is stated on the page.

This is only an acknowledgments page — no table of contents, no FAQ, no price — where Andy Grove thanks his family, "Matthew Powers, a.k.a. Mr. Powers, for inspiring me to write this book in the first place," and "the countless people who have interacted with me over the past six years as I worked on the DataFusion project, especially the Apache Arrow and Apache DataFusion PMC members, committers, and contributors." The one nugget: "This book is also available for purchase in ePub, MOBI, and PDF format" from leanpub.com/how-query-engines-work, copyright © 2020-2026.

Building small, sharp tools — "minimalist, composable programs that worked in concert to a degree of effectiveness that was more than the sum of their parts" — is a Unix philosophy, documented in Eric S. Raymond's *The Art of Unix Programming* (Rules of Modularity, Composition, and Parsimony), that carries over naturally to building modern web platforms and service-oriented microservices. The catch is that a tool can be too small: "the pressure to keep interface complexity and codebase size down, may lead right to a manularity trap — the user has to maintain all the shared context himself," so Raymond's Rule of Minimality says to "choose the shared context you want to manage, and build your programs as small as those boundaries will allow." Brandur got this wrong with a separate organization service built on the existing Heroku API — the private API surface swelled and shallow integration made new features painful across both components, so it was re-integrated, because "although each service was kept fairly simple with the separation, the sum of their complexity was much greater than that of the integrated system."

http.dev lays out HTTP as "the foundation of data exchange on the web," walking through how the request-response model works, the evolution from the original single-line 0.9 spec through HTTP/1.0, 1.1, 2, and 3 (which "replaced TCP with QUIC, a UDP-based transport with built-in encryption"), and the three core building blocks of headers, methods, and status codes. Security gets its own section — plain HTTP transmits cleartext, HTTPS layers TLS on top, and CORS, CSP, session cookies, and Authentication coordinate trust — followed by a long "See also" index linking out to individual topics like ALPN, Oblivious HTTP, WebDAV, and WebTransport.

Kimaki is "a collaborative agent orchestrator that lets you drive every feature of OpenCode from Discord" — each Discord channel is a project, each thread is a coding session, and you install it with `npx -y kimaki@latest` or try the bot in the Kimaki Discord Server. It connects to OpenCode so that "you can use your existing Claude Pro/Max and ChatGPT/Codex subscriptions instead of paying per token," with setup taking about a minute via gateway mode or a self-hosted bot you create yourself. The source lives on GitHub, and the page notes it's "the tool I actually use every day."

MotherDuck is "The Cloud Data Warehouse Built on DuckDB" — fast, serverless analytics with "an isolated compute instance for every person, dashboard, and agent," called Ducklings, spun up in milliseconds. It's built for builders and teams who want to "build a data stack in one prompt, or plug into the one you have," with Flights for Python pipelines, Guides as "the context layer for agents," Dives for agent-built visualizations, and MCP, CLI, and REST interfaces. No pricing or free tier is shown on this page.

Lisse is a small JavaScript library that draws squircle corners, the same continuous curve Figma and iOS use, with bindings for React, Vue, and Svelte plus a framework-agnostic core. Per-corner control, borders, and shadows are included, and the demo shows "how far the squircle pulls in from the CSS-rounded back."

Being good at building and being good at shipping are two separate skills — in the short term they're "actually countervailing." Gifted programmers and writers freeze up because their taste is why their work disappoints them, but "you can typically improve a bad diff with time and effort. You can't improve no diff," so "you have to grit your teeth and ship it." You can't predict what will resonate, so you produce a high volume of work and stay momentum-based rather than outcome-based.

A designer from Villena, Alicante, based in beautiful California, building fun things at SpaceXAI — photography is his longest-running hobby, guitar a close second. "Having fun" lists UnicodeKit ("Browsing characters like it's 1988"), Stray characters, Papercups, a Figma Orgchart plugin ("I promise I'm fun at parties"), and GitHub Actions including Figma → Website ("Should designers code?") and Weekly Update ("It does what it says on the tin"). The feed runs from "A little bit of character" and "Imperfection" back through notes on weekly-update-action labels and "Design advice from Bill Hader."

This library lets you draw marker strokes over web text — "an actual stroke off a nib: ink that pools where a line starts and stops, streaks left behind as it dries, a little bleed past the last letter" — with three nibs, a broad chisel, a rounded bullet and a fine point. It never touches your text: the marks are painted on top, so the words stay selectable and searchable and a mark you put down holds its place through scrolling and a resize, and laying one over another darkens the overlap the way two real passes would. The library itself is small and runs anywhere, with bindings for React, Vue and Svelte when you want them (npm install @highlighters/core, @highlighters/react, @highlighters/vue, @highlighters/svelte).

celld keeps the Durable Objects programming model and gives you control over where cells run, how their state is stored, and how you investigate failures. It's "a stateful distributed system built on S3": Workers handle requests, while Durable Objects, KV, Queues, D1, and Workflows keep state in cells, each with its own SQLite database, and the fleet needs "no membership protocol, failure detector, or consensus service." Self-hosting puts you in charge of your nodes, bucket provider, and operations, but it doesn't guarantee reliability.

the senior engineer death spiral is the most common failure mode he's seen: you tell yourself you need to cosplay a more senior engineer, disappear for weeks, give the "positive update" that you'll "have something to show you quite soon," then try to do a month's work in a week and hope no one notices — until you burn out, get PIP'd, or quit. the fix is counterintuitive: "drop a level," assume everyone around you is operating in good faith, do the bugs and grunt work nobody's gotten to, and move from an outcome-based mindset to a momentum-based one. "big projects are not done with big efforts" — it's slow, steady, incremental work until it's muscle memory, because "you are in the reputation-building business, and software is actually downstream of that."

Knap turns data into Markdown: "Add variables inline with Markdown. Filters modify values and formatting." You can "Generate Markdown from Knap templates" from the CLI — `npx knap render template.md --data data.json --output note.md` — or "Add Knap templating to your app using the API" with `npm install knap`. It also points to the Obsidian Web Clipper ("Save web pages to Markdown with customizable templates") and Obsidian Importer ("Convert data from many apps and file formats to portable Markdown files").

Cactus builds Automation Foundation Models: sub-30MB binaries that put "on-device intelligence on any hardware" — mobile, wearables, AR glasses, smart homes, robotics, automotive, laptops, game consoles, TVs, microcontrollers. Latest releases are Needle 3, "a single 8–29 MB binary that beats models 10× its size on mobile tool calls," and Whistle, a 16.9 MB open speech recognition model supporting seven languages on CPU only. Models use sub-2-bit quantization, run CPU-only and offline, and use hybrid routing where a confidence score "decides whether a request stays on the device or goes to the cloud."

AtAt is your agent, in any app: type @@ in any editable, non-secure text field on your Mac, and let TabTab complete your next words right where you type. Without an agent it's still a full screenshot tool, a searchable clipboard history on ⌘⇧V, and a small action bar for any text you select; Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Cursor, Pi, Hermes, OpenCode, and Antigravity work out of the box, plus your own OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, or DeepSeek key, Ollama, and Siri AI. Requires an Apple silicon Mac running macOS 15+, starts with 7 days free, then $59 yearly or $169 once for lifetime, with a 30-day refund promise, and history stays on your Mac by default with optional iCloud Sync.

Finding problems worth solving as a staff engineer isn't separate from the rest of the job — instead of staring at a blank page trying to "think strategically," Lalit acts like a sponge, absorbing the day-to-day problems people talk about and letting them pile up until connections appear. Waiting is a superpower, but "a common shape is only a hypothesis and elegance is not evidence," so he pressure-tests with prototypes, RFCs, 1:1s and talks before committing — and sometimes the honest answer is to stop. Solving useful problems brings him into more conversations, and that loop makes the next one easier to find.

boat is "the cheapest, most powerful sandbox for agents, built for agent factories" — a persistent Ubuntu VM per agent with SSH and SCP, Docker inside, its own IPv4 or IPv6, a 60fps virtual desktop, and fast disk-level forking from a snapshot, pre-loaded with Docker, VS Code, Chrome, Ghostty, the GitHub CLI, Rust, Node.js and Bun and driven by a CLI built for agents, programmatic use, and humans. "Pay only for the sandboxes you run, billed by the second, with a $20 minimum per month" after a 7-day free trial (25 compute hours), in three sizes — small (2 vCPU / 4 GB) at 0.5x, default (4 vCPU / 8 GB) at 1x, large (8 vCPU / 16 GB) at 2x — with EU regions today and self-serve plans scaling from 100 to 2,000 active sandboxes per account.

Equals is a "single source of truth for the entire team. Same question? Same answer." — an AI analytics tool that "syncs your team's tools to a managed warehouse" ("all your GTM data synced and cleaned in a Snowflake instance we run for you"), adds a spreadsheet layer ("a calculation layer that's easy to audit, trust, and collaborate on") and AI agents, so you "build once, iterate for years." It's for the people named on the page: a RevOps Analyst at a Series C startup, a Head of RevOps at an AI company, a Founder at a Series A startup, a CRO, VP Finance — teams that want to "wire your numbers into how your company operates. A system, not an artifact," pushing briefs to Slack and email, embedding live charts in Notion, and pushing calculated values back into the CRM. "Any agent connects over MCP to analyze the metrics your team trusts—not numbers it invented."

Building agents is still messy: "SDK abstractions break once you hit real tool use," and the author would not again adopt something like the Vercel AI SDK for an agent loop, since the right abstraction isn't clear and provider-side tools and cache control fight the unification. Explicit caching ("I've fully come around and now vastly prefer explicit cache management") makes cost and utilization more predictable, while reinforcement after every tool call, isolating failures in subagents, a file-system-like shared state so tools have no dead ends, and an output tool all end up doing more heavy lifting than expected — and a better tool caller is cheaper in a loop than a cheaper model. Testing and evals are the hardest problem of all, and "at the moment we haven't found something that really makes us happy."

You don’t know what people want — you don’t share their job, obsession, or context — so stop saying what people already have, what you’ve built, or what you fantasize about, and throw the old positioning playbooks in the trash. Position around their aspirations, desired outcomes, and requirements; say what people want in plain words, because desires are more stable than buzzwords and “once you get established as the way of doing something, it’s harder for competitors to displace you.” If you nail it, “the analysts and investors will redefine or name new categories on your behalf, so you never have to bother.”

Scritto is a JavaScript library that animates text in place: give an element a new value and only the characters that changed move — "each one rolls from the old character to the new one while the rest hold their position." It works on numbers, words, and emoji, with bindings for React, Vue, Svelte, and Solid, and a core that runs without a framework. The page also counts up its own traffic as it happens — "You're the 3337th visitor."

Delta is "a multiplayer environment for coding with agents," where "the unit of work is a thread: the conversation with an agent and the checkout of the repository it works in, kept together as one shareable artifact," and you can open it from the desktop or web, or move to a cloud runner. DeltaDB is "the version control layer underneath Delta" — "where Git captures a snapshot at each commit, DeltaDB records work as a stream of fine-grained deltas," each with a stable identity, "so a reference anchors to a change rather than a line number and survives as the code moves."

Meet Okara, the AI CMO — "The only AI CMO you need for growth and marketing," with 10+ marketing agents running 24/7 that research your product first, then execute channel by channel across SEO, Reddit, X, LinkedIn, GEO and more, publishing straight into WordPress, Webflow, Framer, Wix, Sanity, GitHub and the rest of your stack. "Free to start · No credit card required," and it frames itself as "The $14,000/mo job from $129/mo" — replacing a full-time marketing hire, SEO agency, content writer and community growth, for solo devs, bootstrapped founders and teams of two or three.

One of the most valuable things you could do for your software business is talk to your users, but many don’t respond. Netlify cut its onboarding email by 90% — from 150+ words to 14 — and reply rates went from 1% to 8%, because "That’s the power of saying less." Take your welcome or onboarding email, cut out any text that isn’t necessary, take out another 50%, and A/B test positive replies.

Code review will die, unit tests might die too, and the craft of writing code will disappear — "there are still Italian shoe makers around. But look at your feet" — while the craft of building software will be more important than ever. Most bugs won't be coding bugs but "you asked for the wrong thing" bugs, the terminal is dead, tokens are the new computing paradigm, open source in its current form doesn't make sense anymore, and the PM/Design/Eng triad will disappear. "It'll take a while for this to play out" — but do you want to have that job?
This one is thin: the page shows only the title "Learn Harness Engineering" and the word "Loading...", so there's no lesson, table of contents, FAQ, or price to report. Nothing else has rendered yet.

Meet Jan: "Your personal intelligence. Run any model, your way." It's free and open source — "7M+ downloads" and "built in public" — because "we believe AI should be open, and grow through the people who build and use it," with v0.8.6 now live on GitHub.

Models.dev is "An open-source database of AI models" — a single table listing models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI and others, with columns for lab, number of providers, context and output size, reasoning, tool call, structured output, temperature, whether weights are Open or Closed, price, release and updated dates. Rows range from free ($0.00 / $0.00) to $140.00 / $540.00, and the table closes with "No rows match the current search."

I am obsessed with smooth corners - squircles. CSS gave me a radius and nothing else, and no browser drew a real curve; corner-shape ships a superellipse, 'which is not the shape Apple's icons actually draw.' So I built Lisse to draw the right one - a Bezier eased into an arc - with clip-path, SVG borders and shadows, caching, a corne.rs site, and a Chrome and Firefox extension; it's early, open source, MIT.

Wellmade is "a home for well made creative work" — a grid of images from makers, with pieces like an "early identity concept," a "brand identity for pera," and a post titled "All In." A visitor scrolls a feed of that work, each image linking through to the person who made it.

Learn Inference is an interactive companion to *Inference Engineering* by Philip Kiely that covers “everything that happens afterward” — serving generative models in production, from “attention kernels at one end, GPU procurement across three clouds at the other.” It follows the book’s structure with rewritten explanations and simulators, like chapter 1’s time-to-first-token versus tokens-per-second demo, but the page is thin: the chapter list shows only a Glossary, “Every term, defined once,” and there’s no pricing or FAQ.

The tools demand expertise, yet they circumvent the friction that cultivates it — so the path to becoming an expert is closing for the developers being told to accelerate with them. Novices who leaned hardest on AI "finished with an 'illusion of competence' rather than true understanding," while the ones who performed best greatly mitigated or outright ignored the assistance; use the models instead for "interactive documentation, dynamic tutorial generators, and Socratic exercises," since "the most productive learning that can happen with an AI coding tool is when it isn't used to generate much of any code at all." Expertise comes from getting "painfully stuck," so the prescription is friction first — otherwise Sam Altman's vision of selling intelligence back to us on a meter becomes reality.

"LLM Inference Handbook is your technical glossary, guidebook, and reference - all in one," covering everything from Time to First Token and Tokens per Second to continuous batching, prefix caching, GPU architecture, and deployment patterns like BYOC and on-prem, plus practical guidance for deploying, scaling, and operating LLMs in production. It was written because inference knowledge is fragmented — "buried in academic papers, scattered across vendor blogs, hidden in GitHub issues" — and much of it "assumes you already understand half the stack." It ships with interactive calculators, simulators, and visualizers (LLM Inference Visualizer, KV Cache Memory Calculator, Batching Strategy Simulator, and more), and is meant to be read start-to-finish or treated like a lookup table: "There's no wrong way to navigate."

"Your team and agents, in the same room." hilos is a team chat where agents are members — ask for a change in a channel and agents ship real PRs, other agents review, people approve. It's free, and agents run on your machine, on your own account.

effect-mq ships "schema-typed payloads, swappable storage, and at-least-once execution in one package" — jobs are schemas, handlers are Effects, workers are Layers, and interruption, retries, and timeouts "run on the Effect runtime instead of bolted-on process machinery." Storage is a seam ("Postgres through your drizzle schema, Redis through atomic Lua scripts, memory for tests"), with a producer/runner split where "enqueueing never requires a Worker, and the type system enforces it." Install it with `bun add effect-mq` — "or npm / pnpm / yarn."

If you hop between repositories all day you end up memorizing clunky incantations — `rust fmt`, `mix deps.update`, `./gradlew build` or `mvn`, `yarn` or `npm` or `pnpm` — when you'd rather just say *"build the code"*, *"lint it"*, *"format it"*, *"run migrations"*. A small bash script you drop at the repo root (`run build`, `run test`, `run format`) does the trick, and if you want something sturdier there's `make` (declare your targets `.PHONY`, mind the tabs), `just` (Make's familiar shape minus the weirder parts), or `mise`, whose `mise.toml` has grown it into a developer's swiss army knife. "It's super simple to set up and yet it's something I rarely see in the wild."

Now that agents can both hack up code for a specific use and manage the nightly rebase of local changes on top of upstream releases, agents change the ROI on customizing software on two fronts simultaneously — and "software that can be personalized doesn't need a plugin system or a config file." A single prompt built meat.dev into Shelley (the bespoke software this blog is written in), doing pre-processing a VS Code extension API or vimdiff could never manage, because "The source code is the extension system." For end-user products to make sense in a company today, they need to be personalizable, "which means we need the source code" — and that's where Claude Code hits a wall: "It is closed-source software, so you don't get to personalize it."

Wondering turns anything you want to learn, "from LLMs to quantum mechanics to product design," into a personalized course of three-minute lessons with visuals, podcasts, and interactive exercises. It's built for curious people as "a better habit than doomscrolling," gamified with daily streaks, friend streaks, XP, and streak freezes, plus spaced repetition across everything you learn (scheduled with the FSRS algorithm) and an AI tutor to discuss anything. You can explore public courses shared by the Wondering community or download it for iPhone.

The Pudding publishes numbered visual data stories "about just about everything" — mowing experiments, k-pop generations, IVF journeys, dicing onions — each stamped with an issue number and month, running from #200 Mar 2025 deep into #225 Oct 2026. "Get The Pudding in your inbox" points readers to the newsletter, and a merch note says "If you like our stories, you'll love our merch." No editors or writers are named on the page.

Hatchet is "the orchestration engine for teams who ship": write tasks and workflows as code with retries, scheduled and cron runs, event and webhook triggers, durable tasks, DAGs, priorities, rate limits, and fair scheduling, then run workers in your own cloud while the engine is a managed service or self-hosted. It's "Fully MIT-licensed" and self-hostable ("a single CLI command away"), with native SDKs for TypeScript, Python, and Go, and use cases spanning AI agents, background tasks, data ingestion, and webhooks and events.

AI can do more every day, but deciding what it should do is up to us — and because productive knowledge is tacit, local, fleeting, and held privately by those who acquired it through their work, intelligence alone isn't enough outside domains like chess and math. So the future worth building is human: strong models, tools that let people fine-tune weights with their own knowledge, and interaction models for live multimodal collaboration, with "alignment as a feature not of a single model but of an ecosystem of AIs raised in different places." The trade-offs the industry assumes — participation vs. capability, ownership vs. safe alignment — are technical challenges to solve, not choices to make.

Feather is an inbox that "sorts, merges, and surfaces insights, on its own" — it "removes what's done, keep what matters, and nudges what needs you." No pricing, free tier, or open-source status is shown on the page.

Articles is a directory of bookmarks — link after link, each with its title and a line of description lifted from the source. It points to things like "Natural language as source code, conventional code as a build artifact," "118 million queries per second on Neki," "A year of drawing, testing, and shipping a complete icon system," and "Bored People Quit."

I'm still using coding assistants on my personal projects, but letting them roam free leaves me with a colossal amount of cognitive debt, and poring over hundreds of lines of overly-defensive, badly-commented, subtly incorrect AI PRs is not fun. So my agents files say "Never create, edit, move, rename, or delete project files unless I explicitly ask you to do so" — instead the LLM shows every edit in chat and I type it in manually, which makes me 2x faster instead of 10x, but builds a spatial map of my codebase, forces me to slow down and catch hallucinations, and lets me refactor as I go. It's the same advice experienced programmers gave me as a teenager about never copy-pasting code: I value comprehension over productivity, because the industry is taking on cognitive debt we'll have to pay back very soon.

"Break down CSS backgrounds, layer by layer" — paste any background CSS into the playground and bg.layers shows what each layer contributes, separately. Radial, conic, and linear layers are listed individually, and you can drag to reorder them.

Postgres intelligence for AI agents & apps, because 'Nobody reads database metrics. pgbot does.' Connect your Postgres and get answers, not dashboards: what's healthy, what's broken, and what to fix first, with AI-powered explanations and a read-only open-source agent that speaks MCP as a tool.

Iris is "A camera for coding agents." One fast command or MCP tool call produces one trustworthy image, rendering with your real installed Chrome over the DevTools Protocol. It's MIT licensed, installs with curl or cargo install iris-screenshot, and includes a local stdio MCP server that exposes the one capture tool.

Pullfrog is "a GitHub bot that runs AI agents on your repo" — it listens for GitHub events like PRs opened, issues created, reviews submitted, and CI failures and triggers agent runs based on your configuration, or you can just mention `@pullfrog` to assign tasks. It's open source and model-agnostic — "Works with any LLM provider: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI, Mistral, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, and more" or the Claude Pro/Max, ChatGPT Codex, Grok, Kimi Code, or OpenCode Go plan you already pay for — and all agent runs happen in your repo's GitHub Actions via a special `pullfrog.yml` workflow. Personal accounts and public repositories stay free with no per-seat charges, Organization is $30/month with a 14-day trial and no card required, and Enterprise is custom.

A border-radius is just a number, and the number is not enough: roundness is relative, so a button, a card and a panel should not blindly share one token, and a value near half the height "doesn't commit" — the button reads swollen instead of soft. For nested corners, derive the inner radius instead of retyping it — outer radius minus the full gap, with the border counted as part of that gap — then look, because "the formula gets you to a clean relationship, not a finished design." Drop the formula when the curve changes: squircle does not offset to a smaller squircle, and "squircles take the floor away," so judge the result, ship the least-wrong one, and gate corner-shape behind @supports.

Silicon Valley once celebrated “the crazy ones, the misfits and rebels who saw things differently,” but it “now seems to have found a new kind of crazy that isn’t born of rebellion but fear of falling behind.” A couple earning a combined $550,000 a year still feels behind because someone at Anthropic might buy the dream house first, and a founder has Claude review recordings of her first dates to judge whether she was engaging enough. Technology was supposed to make room for life, yet “every ‘saved’ hour is returned to a race with no finish line” — so perhaps falling behind is not the worst thing that could happen, and we need the misfits who know when to stop.

A LessWrong poster in AI safety, believing "there is a shortage of generalists in the community," assembled a reading list of the essays and blog posts that have personally helped them the most — 18 documents to start, with an open call for others to comment with pieces they think should be on this list. "The crux of this reading list is the idea that if you're working hard as a generalist on a project you care a lot about, then by rigorously applying the lessons from these documents you will improve more quickly than you otherwise would," and the items are grouped into dispositional characteristics, strategy, project leadership, and interpersonal/organizational understanding, leaning repeatedly on Paul Graham (5), Ben Kuhn (4), Ethan Perez (2), and Greg Brockman (2).

The mind that builds software is far smaller than the software it builds — four slots, a narrow beam, and a leak — so a warning half of attentive people look straight at and miss "isn't really a warning. It's a decoration," and a system built for an operator who never gets tired "is already broken. It just hasn't had its bad day yet." LLMs turn out to share the same boundedness, "only now it's running in silicon," since a context window is a hard limit and models lose the middle of long inputs, so the central question isn't how to find a bigger mind but "how do we shape the thing so that a small mind can work on it without bringing it all down." Nearly everything we call good engineering is an answer to that — names, boundaries, tests, undo move facts out of the fragile four-slot mind into the structure — and designing for the most constrained user, as with OXO's peeler, "just gives you a better thing."

Nautilus is Science Connected, publishing stories across History, Biology, Arts, Math, and Communication, including a piece by poet Will Dowd, from 'This Is the Oldest Peace Treaty Ever Discovered' to 'The Elegance of a Stupid Question.' It also invites readers to 'Read Stories from Our Newest Print Issue: The Stupid Issue.'

Essays by Maggie Appleton, running from "A Brief History & Ethos of the Digital Garden" — "a newly revived philosophy for publishing personal knowledge on the web" — and "The Pattern Language of Project Xanadu" to "The Dark Forest and Generative AI" and "A Treatise on AI Chatbots Undermining the Enlightenment" on "chatbot sycophancy, passivity, and the case for more intellectually challenging companions." Along the way: digital anthropology as "a discipline at the intersection of cultural anthropology and binary logic," bi-directional links, transclusion, databases, and "the strange experience of growing a human from scratch, without any conscious understanding of how you are doing it."

Are.na Editorial is "Essays, interviews, and other forms of writing from and about the Are.na community" — the page itself shows only placeholder posts, each titled "An Example Post Title" with lorem ipsum body text and dated "January 1, 0000 by Example Author." No cadence, subscription details, or named editors appear on the page.

The most effective way to build software and get massive adoption is no longer high quality mainline apps but via building blocks that enable and encourage others to build quantity over quality — Ghostty hit a million daily macOS update checks in 18 months, and libghostty hit multiple millions of daily users in 2. Because the factory of today is agentic and AI is *really good* at gluing together high quality, well documented, and proven components, the barrier to entry that once limited the ecosystem is gone, which lowers the quality bar, spreads awareness, lowers maintenance burden, and outsources R&D. The point is the shift has already happened. We're living in it.

Flows is "product adoption infrastructure that lets modern teams build anything, no-code or all-code" — product tours, workflows, and in-product surveys (NPS, CSAT, PMF, CES), built with your own components and open-source SDKs so your design system stays intact. Independent analysis of AI: understand the AI landscape to choose the best model and provider for your use case, comparing models side-by-side on intelligence, pricing, speed, latency, and benchmarks. Across 30,954 people mowing the same lawn, the median hit 91% efficiency, 52% came within five moves of optimal, and 16% did it perfectly—but the real split came down to one decision: the best mowers anticipated the dead end, mowed the right side first so they could end on the left, and spent their thinking at the forks instead of reacting later. As lawns got bigger, optimality held around 90%, not because people thought longer (time alone explains less than 5% of the variation), but because they decomposed the lawn into smaller sections, compressed patterns into a mental model, and used a good heuristic: spend your attention on the decisions that matter and nothing on the ones that don’t. So it’s not about thinking more or faster, but when thinking happens.

Modem discovers and organizes your customer concerns across support threads, sales calls, community posts, social comments, and your own data via API, groups every mention of the same issue into one topic linked to the tickets and PRs fixing it, and hands the whole story to people and agents with sources attached. Product, engineering, customer success, and sales all work from the same record of what customers said and what shipped—less digging, more shipping—via dashboard, agent, plugins & MCP, CLI, and HTTP API. Free is $0/mo for 2,500 events + limited agent usage; Startup is $80/mo for 15,000 events + extended agent usage; Scale is $250/mo for 60,000 events + highest agent usage, free for 14 days; Enterprise is custom volume and retention, SAML/Advanced SSO, SLAs, and dedicated support, with unlimited users on every plan.

A new study that my colleagues and I conducted suggests that how much sugar you consumed before your second birthday could shape your health decades later – even into your 70s. Using Britain's postwar sugar rationing as a natural experiment – consumption nearly doubled when rationing ended in September 1953 – the researchers found that people born between 1951 and 1956 who spent longer stretches of their first 1,000 days under rationing had lower incidence of breast, prostate, liver, rectal and lung cancer (liver cancer rates around 69% lower, breast 36% lower) and longer telomeres, "equivalent to about 2.2 years of slower biological ageing." What is most surprising, however, is not the cancer results or the biological markers of ageing but that "people who experienced sugar rationing early in life still consumed less sugar in adulthood, around age 50" – a taste for less sweetness, formed early, seems to stick.

One connected system" — POST /orders calls orders::create through iii, then the API calls database::execute through iii. A numbered list of 95 reasons to have your own website — "to write for oneself," "to have a home on the open web," "to keep the like counter at 0," "to bring web rings back," "to own what you publish," "because vibe coding only gets you so far," "to publish without social pressure" — each reason often linked out to someone else's site as proof. So this article trains your ability to spot what's wrong, name it, and fix it: each exercise shows two animations side by side, and your job is to pick the better one, write down why you chose it, then see his breakdown — because "putting into words why something feels right trains your ability to articulate your judgment, a skill that will be incredibly valuable in the AI era."

There's no secret silver bullet to performance — Linear is fast because it's "built from the ground up on the right foundation, then improved by countless decisions." The server is a sync target rather than a source of truth, the database lives in the browser, mutations apply locally first and reconcile in the background, and the first load ships less code in more pieces with a service worker precaching the rest. Engineering speed makes a single interaction fast, design speed makes the path to each interaction short.

The question "am I a writer?" had bothered me for years, and taking it seriously — through Brand's *How Buildings Learn*, Darwin's *Origin*, and Einstein's 1905 relativity paper — shows that new creative identities emerge from near-amateur work on fundamental questions existing fields don't take seriously, work that demands "novel combinations of tools, giving rise to a unique written form." Because such questions sit outside or on the border of existing fields, forging those identities often requires leaving existing communities and "becoming illegible even to oneself for a time" — Brand writes to explore, Darwin writes with a goal, and Einstein's results work as "a kind of interface or API" reused everywhere. Stories do something else again: *Lolita*, Ted Chiang's "Story of Your Life", and the Bible don't hand you reusable conclusions but an experience, occasionally "new states of consciousness," which is why good story and good explanation are very different things.

The product you work on matters more than the title on your badge — frontend engineers should work where the frontend *is* the product, and backend engineers should work where the server is. He maps products on a complexity matrix (thin/thick client × thin/thick server) and says you want to be in the ambitious thick-client, thick-server quadrant — Figma, Google Docs, Spotify — where "everyone here is solving hard problems." The laws I keep coming back to — Fitts, Hick, Miller, Doherty, Postel — aren't really about interfaces, they're about how people work: how we perceive time, how we make decisions, how much we can hold in our heads at once. Make the things people need to click easy to click, show what matters now and reveal complexity when it's needed, chunk data instead of showing blobs, keep interactions under 400ms or make them feel fast, and validate generously while formatting strictly. "At the end of the day, the hardest thing to do is make something feel easy, and that's what were trying to achieve."

Over the course of this article, I'll explain the workings of the mechanism seen in the demonstration below — the *movement*, the inner part of a mechanical watch that's usually enclosed in a metal case, since "beautiful watch cases merely hide the intricate mechanisms which are the real stars of the show." The timekeeping system "consists of just seven major elements," and I walk through each one: the mainspring and barrel that store the energy, the gear train that turns a few barrel rotations into thousands of hand rotations, the escapement that lets the escape wheel briefly *escape* from its jail, and the balance wheel that "forms the beating heart of a watch." Because "as instruction count increases, instruction-following quality decreases uniformly" and Claude Code's own system prompt already carries ~50 instructions, less is more: keep the file concise and universally applicable (consensus says under 300 lines; HumanLayer's root file is under sixty), push task-specific detail into separate self-descriptive docs you point Claude at via progressive disclosure, and "never send an LLM to do a linter's job." Design keeps being misunderstood in our industry, where new tools promise to generate interfaces faster — but "the hard part of design is rarely generating the form," it is understanding the problem well enough to know what should exist at all. Drawing on Christopher Alexander's idea of design as the search for a good fit between form and context, the argument is that bad design is where unresolved forces remain, and AI makes this worse: it generates plausible outputs quickly instead of helping you understand the underlying problem, producing products that "look polished, ambitious, and impressive at first glance" but unravel the moment you use them. That is why designing visually still beats prompting — the value is not only in the output but in the gradual understanding that comes through doing the work.

The blog covers a deep dive into ASCII rendering with shape vectors, WebGL gradients and shader math, the web's clipboard APIs, compressing Icelandic name declension into a 3.27 kB trie, planes in 3D space, TypeScript's structural typing (and why it doesn't properly type Object.keys), and the engineering behind Figma's vector networks. Generative AI can produce things with utility—and a Washington Department of Ecology job listing that uses AI for boilerplate and test generation is "hard to argue against"—but utility isn't the only kind of value a thing can have. A hand-knitted scarf or a screenplay written for a brother carries meaning because "choosing to spend a fraction of our most precious resource for someone else is the strongest signal we can send that that person matters to us," and since "by making us more productive, AI eliminates meaning," the author aims to use AI for utilitarian goods and put "as much of myself and as little of the machine into it as I can" when human connection matters.

Repeated exposure kills novelty — "Novelty is the equivalent of an exclamation mark," and like semantic satiation, extravagant motion on common actions eventually stops meaning anything. Stealing the three color rule from cinematography, he argues for making 90% of an experience familiar and 10% novel, saving the flourish for once-only moments: onboarding, the first Home Screen unlock, a Stripe Press-style microsite whose novelty "hits hard because most of the pages aren't such experiences." Frequency isn't the only variable — intent matters, and there's a "novelty tax" that means how much you can get away with depends on your ambition and an audience that's receptive to, or even seeking, novelty. "Make most things familiar, do something unexpected."

Most components are built for the happy path, and "The real test isn't whether your component works on your current page. It's whether it works when someone else uses it—in conditions you didn't plan for." The answer is to make it server-proof, hydration-proof, instance-proof, concurrent-proof, composition-proof, portal-proof, transition-proof, activity-proof, leak-proof, and future-proof — because "These aren't edge cases. They're the new normal."

Using AI agents correctly is a process of reviewing code: LLMs are good at producing a lot of code, but they don't have the depth of judgement of a competent software engineer, so "left unsupervised, they will spend a lot of time committing to bad design decisions." The biggest mistake engineers make in code review is "only thinking about the code that was written, not the code that *could have been* written" — a nitpicky reviewer will bikeshed lines and miss guiding the AI away from architectural dead ends, while a rubber-stamp reviewer will put too much trust in it.

Loop engineering is "replacing yourself as the person who prompts the agent" — you design the system that finds the work, hands it out, checks it, remembers what's done and decides the next thing, instead of holding the tool one turn after the other. A loop needs five pieces (automations, worktrees, skills, plugins/connectors, sub-agents) plus memory that lives outside the conversation, and since Codex and Claude Code now ship all five, "once you notice the shape is the same you stop arguing about which tool." But the loop "changes the work, it does not delete you from it": verification is still on you, comprehension debt grows faster, and the comfortable posture is cognitive surrender — so "build the loop. Stay the engineer."

After a year of coding agents, the argument is that we've traded discipline and agency for an addiction to producing the largest amount of code in the shortest time, and now software feels like a brittle mess: agents make the same booboos over and over, have no human bottleneck, and their local, low-recall search compounds complexity into an unrecoverable mess. Use agents only for scoped, non-mission-critical work with a closed loop and you as the final quality gate, because 'slowing the fuck down is the way to go': write architecture and API by hand, limit daily generated code to what you can review, and stay in the code. 'All of this requires discipline and agency; all of this requires humans.'

At the center of any movement on the web is an easing curve—the “rhythm” of the movement—and understanding `cubic-bezier` curves, usually curved lines defined by four numeric values, is the goal of improving our own animations and UIs. Movement tells a story: well-designed movement makes a UI both more engaging and more intuitive, while bad transitions and animations can make the same UI feel mediocre, cheap, confusing, or even broken. “The transition itself is the verb; the easing curve is the adverb.”

You can do real research — "actual research that produces insights you can't find anywhere else" — in the margins of a full-time job, because the constraint isn't credentials or time, it's knowing how to scope questions, extract maximum value from minimum reading, and build knowledge that compounds. So define the question tightly and set the definition of done before you start, prioritize the two or three seminal sources over ten mediocre ones, stop when the same themes keep recurring, and write notes in your own words with context so the ideas stay available years later. Then synthesize across domains by spotting patterns, translating concepts between fields, and using outsider advantages — and treat each project as an experiment whose errors are your teachers.

Slop creep is 'death by a thousand reasonable decisions': no single commit is wrong, but coding agents remove the old circuit breaker because they don’t see the system, they see the prompt, and build 'confidently, competently wrong' abstractions that calcify. The fix is not to stop using agents but to spend far more time in the plan—write code snippets for key data models and abstractions, review every line—so the agent fills gaps instead of walking through one-way doors alone; otherwise codebase slop becomes product slop and users leave.

A "living doc: notes and resources" from Flo, "a designer who builds" who is now "tinkering at Paradigm as our founding design engineer," pointing to pieces on defining the role, guidelines and agent skills, interesting tools, resources, courses purchased, design pattern libraries, communities, and personal perspectives. Its own notes argue that "material understanding beats tool proficiency" and that "design engineering streamlines the creation process, minimizing back-and-forth."

Transactions are "a sequence of actions that we want to perform on a database as a single, atomic operation," and this article walks through how Postgres and MySQL each deliver consistent reads — Postgres via multi-versioning of rows (with `VACUUM FULL` to purge the duplicates) and MySQL via an undo log that reconstructs past versions on the fly. It lays out the four isolation levels from **Serializable** down to **Read Uncommitted**, naming the phenomena each permits — phantom reads, non-repeatable reads, and the ``dirty read,'' which is ``really bad!'' — then contrasts concurrent writes: MySQL's shared and exclusive row-level locking (which can deadlock) versus Postgres' predicate locks and optimistic conflict resolution. Both engines kill one transaction to preserve `SERIALIZABLE` guarantees, so ``applications must account for this outcome, and have retry logic for important transactions.''

"I'm not preaching absolute truth but merely some personal preferences and understandings of what makes a good React component." Props shouldn't duplicate context — `<Dialog isOpen>` beats `<Dialog isDialogOpen>` — and if you're adding a boolean prop, consider whether it can be derived from an existing one, because enum props "make impossible states impossible" and `variant="primary"` beats `isPrimary isSecondary`. Composability wins over a `data` prop ("Yikes"), and for high-frequency interactions where nothing else depends on the state, it's more performant to manipulate the DOM directly from the callback than to trigger a re-render.

A rate limiter lets you control the rate of traffic that your service processes by blocking requests that exceed a set limit during a period of time. The post walks through the three most common algorithms: fixed windows (simple and predictable, but "Allows bursts up to 2x the `limit` when requests begin near the end of a window"), sliding windows (smooths traffic for high loads, usually approximated as a floating window since "Storing timestamps for each request is resource-intensive"), and token buckets ("Allows bursts of high traffic, but enforces a long-term average rate of requests"). Plus other considerations: a persisted store like Redis, fail open, sensible keys, and useful 429 errors.

Detail fixes bugs in the background while you ship features — it exercises your code to find thousands of bugs, picks the top 1% you're most likely to care about, and fixes them for you. It's for fast-moving teams "serious about maintaining a high quality bar," ships PRs or tickets to Linear, Jira, or Asana, and is SOC 2 Type II certified with zero data retention. First week free, get started in under 5 minutes.

He's "one of those people who loves hearing 'fun facts' about stuff," so he closes out the year with a pile of them: a team of eight-plus programmers implemented Tetris as a Conway's Game of Life simulation with a full programmable CPU, leap seconds are being abolished by 2035, Vim is Turing complete, and the backslash basically didn't exist in writing before 1930 (it was added to ASCII so mathematicians could write their operators). Other claims: galactic algorithms like Coppersmith-Winograd are theoretically faster but vastly slower at real scales, most pre-2006 mergesort implementations were broken by a midpoint overflow that only bit past a billion elements, PDF's drawing model can't render perfect circles, USBs are supposed to go in logo-side up, and Excel forced biologists to rename 27 genes (Microsoft fixed it three years later). He even corrects one of his own facts on the page: Google Sheets treats 1900 as a normal year, so the Lotus 1-2-3 leap-year backwards-compatibility story no longer holds.

Forma is "your canvas for notes, tasks and anything else" — a native MacOS app where you click and drag to create cards, sketch with the marker tool, and "build any canvas layout you want – project boards, freeform notes, or your own system, right on your Mac." It's for solo creators, designers, and developers who "think visually and want to organize notes and tasks on a canvas rather than in lists." It's not free: a one-time purchase of $9.99 with no subscription, no free trial, sold through the Mac App Store, local-first with iCloud sync on by default.

Patterns.dev is a collection of design patterns grouped into three tracks: JavaScript Patterns "focused on plain Javascript and Node.js" (Singleton, Proxy, Prototype, Observer, Module, Mixin, Mediator/Middleware, Flyweight, Factory, plus loading and performance ones like "Split your code into small, reusable pieces" and "Reduce the bundle size by eliminating dead code"), React Patterns "focused on React and Next.js" (HOC, Render Props, Hooks, Compound, Client-side Rendering through React Server Components, and "A comprehensive guide to building React apps in 2025/2026"), and Vue Patterns (Components, Composables, Provide/Inject, Renderless components, State Management). Each entry is just a title and a one-line description pointing to its page — "Intercept and control interactions to target objects", "Load non-critical components when they are visible in the viewport" — so the page is a table of contents, not prose, with no FAQ or pricing on it.

Great interfaces rarely come from a single thing — "They're usually a collection of small things that compound into a great experience," and Jakub walks through the ones he uses: `text-wrap: balance` on titles paired with `text-wrap: pretty` on descriptions, concentric border radius where the outer radius equals the inner radius plus the padding, animated icons that transition opacity, scale and blur, crisp text via `antialiased`, `tabular-nums` for shifting digits, and interruptible animations since "If animations aren't interruptible, it can make the interface feel broken." He also covers splitting and staggering enter animations with a delay between sections, keeping exit animations subtle so they don't demand the same attention, aligning optically rather than geometrically, using a layered `box-shadow` instead of a border, and adding a 1px outline at 10% opacity to images. Based on reader feedback, he turned the tips into an installable skill: `npx skills add jakubkrehel/make-interfaces-feel-better`.

Letters to a Young Creator is a series published by the Steve Jobs Archive, opening with a Series Introduction and followed by dated letters datelined from Los Angeles, London, New York, Palo Alto, Milan, Osaka, Ebeltoft, Kronberg and more, running from July 2024 through November 2025. No editor, writer, or subscription details appear on the page.

There are nine types of online databases, and all databases have one purpose: to store data so you can retrieve it — which means evaluating them becomes a question of understanding tradeoffs. I evaluate data systems on three dimensions — performance (read, write and space amplification, plus the RUM conjecture), availability (PACELC, where only during a network partition do you choose between availability and consistency), and durability (LCD: you may pick two of latency, cost and durability) — and usage of these frameworks answers how to choose a data system that serves your use case at the acceptable cost, both on hardware requirements and operational overhead.

System Design Classroom is “A System Design Newsletter to help you build better software,” written by Raul Junco. The latest piece is “AI Agents Just Rediscovered the Dual-Write Problem” — “The distributed-systems failure hiding between agent state and the real world” — dated Sep 26. The page also lists 15 recommendations, and shows no cadence or subscription details.

Everyone can ship things today, but "most of what gets shipped cannot *survive*" — and survival isn't about PMF or DAU. Since universal entropy is naturally increasing, simplicity is the best bet: less surface area for decay, and complex products like Photoshop and Linux only last because of "relentless maintenance and deep, irreplaceable value." Make better things rather than more things, and ship slowly — patience compounds, and the "blank time" where you feel not ready is where inspiration grows.

Protocol Cards — Evidence-backed Nervous System Regulation lays out five ways in: Emergency Acute Stress for "Rapid interventions for panic, overwhelm, or acute stress moments," Focus Performance to "Prepare mentally for calls, presentations, or difficult conversations," Recovery Post-Stress, Sleep Wind Down, and Feel Process Emotion. Each is one line and a card — "Click a card to explore protocols." Beyond those five headings there's nothing else on the page, so take it as an index, not a lesson.

Writing code used to be slower than reviewing it, but now the bottleneck has moved downstream — "if input grows faster than throughput, you have an accumulating failure" — and OpenClaw sitting on north of 2,500 open pull requests is what a lot of AI-adjacent open source and "AI-first" internal projects now feel like: no triage, no review, a Starbucks overrun by mobile orders. Review can't really be automated, and if machines can't be accountable then humans still have to understand the output and rubber stamp it in the morning; Pi just throttles the inflow by auto-closing PRs, and the textile industry's lesson looms as "single-use plastic software." "I too am the bottleneck now. But you know what? Two years ago, I too was the bottleneck. I was the bottleneck all along."

When a component exits, React batches the update that closes the popover with the ones that change the exiting component's contents — and "you probably don't care about something that's exiting, but if it updates at the same time it draws attention to itself." What he wanted was a way to tell React to stop committing DOM changes in exiting components, and Suspense already behaves that way — "React continues to render suspended subtrees but doesn't commit their changes to the DOM" — except that it also hides them with `display: none !important`. So he built `Freeze`, a small wrapper around `Suspense` that uses a Fragment ref to undo that style; it works in React 18 & 19.2 and pairs particularly well with React Aria Components, though "it's obviously a bit of a trick" that could break in a future version.

For years Silicon Valley promised AI agents that would automate white-collar work, and the progress was underwhelming—until Claude Code, an Anthropic tool that "just DOES stuff," sent the tech world into a frenzy by booking theater tickets, analyzing DNA, and replicating a Stanford political scientist's paper in an hour. It's "bigger" than the ChatGPT moment—possibly an inflection point on the path to AGI, with Anthropic's Boris Cherny saying Claude now writes 100 percent of his code—but it still sometimes "feels like yelling at a puppy for peeing on your couch," and if it delivers on its biggest supporters' promises, it will be equally disruptive.

A skill that puts "visual proof in every pull request" — it teaches coding agents to show their work with before and after screenshots and video, accessing protected preview deployments and formatting every capture for GitHub. Install it with `npx skills add vercel-labs/before-and-after#main`; browser navigation, authentication, and capture stay with the version-matched skills bundled in `agent-browser`, while "before and after formats the media and publishes it through `gh --attach`."

Boring Avatars is an open-source React library for customizable SVG avatars — `<Avatar colors={["#00686c","#32c2b9","#edecb3","#fad928","#ff9915"]} variant="beam" />`. The page shows one at work in a mock social feed: a placeholder, a liked photo, a designer profile with 1.2M followers · 451 following, and a chat list of names active 3 to 31 min ago.

Just Postgres is a practical guide from Denis Magda, who says he shares what he has learned so you can build better applications. It promises "Everything you need to master Postgres" through four sections: The Book, Blog, Recipes, and YouTube. The Book covers "the breadth and depth of Postgres capabilities," Recipes gives "quick, copy-paste solutions to common Postgres tasks and problems," and YouTube offers "video tutorials and deep dives"—but the page is thin, with no FAQ or pricing.

This is Will Larson's notes on Richard Rumelt's *The Crux*, which he calls "quite good" and better than *Good Strategy, Bad Strategy* at "concisely landing the problem areas to avoid" — though if you had to pick just one, he'd still recommend *Good Strategy, Bad Strategy* first for its structured exploration of problems. The recurring themes that resonate: "Don't start with goals–start by understanding the challenge and finding its crux," and "Don't Confuse Current Financial Results with Strategy," because the numbers always add up but never tell you what to do. The biggest idea for him is the tension between executives working the crux and managing the team and business around them, alongside the difference between Rumelt's challenge-based strategy and his own constraint-based view of engineering strategy.

Pool knows what actually matters, magically links and categorises your content, and lets you organize it in pools and share it with friends. It's downloadable on the App Store, with Research and Careers pages; no pricing, free tier, or open-source status is shown.
