links.summary: I went into this knowing nothing about audio engineering and came out with a library of sounds I understand and can tweak — the process was collaborative, I provided taste and AI provided implementation, and neither of us could have done it alone. What I learned is that sometimes not knowing the technicalities is actually a good thing: using Cursor as a translator helped me turn feelings into logic.

The `archived_at` column approach to soft delete is "simple at first, but in my experience, it's full of pitfalls down the line" — it oozes complexity into queries, indexes, migrations, and restoration code, leaves tables full of dead rows, and bloats backups. Looking at alternatives in PostgreSQL — application-level event archiving, triggers, and WAL-based CDC — "if I were starting a new project today and needed soft delete, I'd reach for the trigger-based approach first. It's simple to set up, keeps live tables clean, and doesn't require extra infrastructure."

Letta argues that evaluating memory tools in isolation is "extremely challenging" because memory quality "depends more on the underlying agentic system's ability to manage context and call tools than on the memory tools themselves." To test it, they dropped LoCoMo conversational history into a plain file attached to a Letta agent with filesystem tools (`grep`, `search_files`, `open`, `close`) and scored 74.0% on LoCoMo with GPT-4o mini, "significantly above Mem0's reported 68.5% score for their top-performing graph variant." The conclusion: "With a well-designed agent, even simple filesystem tools are sufficient to perform well on retrieval benchmarks such as LoCoMo."

A deck of 175+ tactic cards sorted into 12 stacks — onboarding, activation, retention, monetisation and eight more — where each card is "an emotional building block, designed to make your feature land and your app stick." Plays are the individual tactics (33 of them, five cards apiece: the tactic card, a "Make It Yours" prompt card and three real example cards), and the whole thing also ships as "a huge Figma swipe file" with 99+ annotated screens from real apps. Pay once, $97, download it straight away, updates free forever — and it's "not a course. No videos. No BS."

Trails is a directory of trails — each one a name, a terse thesis like "Self-deception as strategy: the best liars believe themselves" or "Rare signals drown in false positives," and the stack of book covers behind it. The trails run from Useful Lies to Mental Maps, through Expert Intuition, Winner's Lock, Proxy Trap, Steel Box, and "why isolated groups lose knowledge and capabilities."

The "X is all you need" hype cycle — "RIP MCP. Long live skills!" — is wrong: Skills are reusable prompts with optional bundled artifacts, MCP is simply a way to expose *new tools* (OAuth-native, permission-scoped, and good for context steering), and "sub-agents are the ignored opportunity" — fully encapsulated, able to run a different model and tools, and resembling the map/reduce pattern. "Commands are dead in my opinion" — they're just a Skill or a subagent with UX on top. His ask is to go try skills and go try some *good* MCP servers, because both have a place, and the fundamental that matters is managing the context window.

Typex is a bare-bones typing drill: "Tippe die Buchstaben ab" followed by letter runs — dalk·salsa·das·flak·als·fall·alks·skala·jklö — with a German QWERTZ key map laid out key by key from Linker Mittelfinger to AltGr. There's no table of contents, no FAQ, no pricing, and nothing else on the page beyond the drill and the keyboard.

After losing the last Lyft bike in Haight-Ashbury one too many times, Ilan spent a month reverse engineering Lyft's private API — Charles Proxy on the iOS traffic, spoofing a Charles root CA to read the SSL, replaying the `rent` endpoint with a faked `userLocation` to slip past the geofence, then brute-forcing 5-digit bike IDs with `asyncio`/`aiohttp` at ~650 RPS in 15 seconds. It worked ("holy shit it worked"), until an intern friend mentioned the sev email — and since Lyft's guidelines call brute-force ineligible, HackerOne only covered the accidental two-bike race condition, which still earned an exception and a $500 bounty. His closing lesson: "Even scary 'physical' systems have digital interfaces you may recognize" — "Go reverse engineer something. Just, be nice about it."

Buttondown's ~2TB core Postgres database — where every newsletter, email, user, and subscriber lives — had been on RDS since the very start, but the AWS Console is "a labyrinth," running on a single replica meant taking the whole app down for config changes, and they were even on slower `gp2` storage. After finding PlanetScale Postgres substantially faster, the migration "ended up being... a learning experience": logical replication was taking many days and hurting RDS, DMS was "will take multiple weeks to copy over data slow," and pgcopydb did the whole copy in about 7 hours once they patched its bugs (a string containing null parsed as a literal null, duplicated single quotes) in their fork — then a scheduled night-of migration and some PgBouncer cleanup got them over. Now PlanetScale's Insights tab has them adding indexes and changing queries, and the automation queueing system's latency dropped 100x (p50 of 100ms to 1ms), with bulk actions processing faster and the internal admin tool no longer timing out.

faster.dev is "a training platform for software developers who want to ship more without turning their codebase into chaos" — structured video series, stand-alone field notes, behind-the-scenes project logs, and downloadable slash commands, skills, and rules "you can use right away." "You already know how to build software. This is the setup, the systems, and the workflows that let you do it faster with AI," for $299/year with a 30-day full refund, no questions asked.

Taste isn't subjective: whatever job people do, they want to do better, and if your job is to design things and there's no such thing as beauty, then there's no way to get better at it — so your old tastes were not merely different, but worse. Once you admit there is such a thing as good and bad design, you can start to study it, and it's surprising how much different fields agree: good design is simple, timeless, solves the right problem, suggestive, hard, looks easy, uses symmetry, resembles nature, is redesign, can copy, is often strange, happens in chunks, and is often daring. "The recipe for great work is: very exacting taste, plus the ability to gratify it."

Paper is a browser-based design tool built intentionally around designers and the design process — "Tools that introduce coding or responsive constraints too early can actually be harmful in that early part of the process." Founder Stephen Haney walks through a stack obsessed with speed: an 8 millisecond frame budget, React bailed out to vanilla JavaScript, MobX, Bun, Hono, MongoDB, and a homemade WebSocket multiplayer system, with handwritten shaders and canvas effects you can copy as running React code.

"Database School is the best place to learn, understand, optimize, and confidently use databases" — 48 hours of content across 391 videos and 7 series (Durable Objects, High Performance SQLite, MySQL for Developers, Intro to Postgres, Mastering Postgres, Advent of SQL, and Convex), pitched at developers who want to "master the core of your stack" without the "computer science jargon." Pricing is an All Access Pass at $269 USD/year or Team Pricing at $1,199 USD/year, with no free trial but free videos in every series, a 30-day money-back guarantee, and lifetime access to Mastering Postgres or High Performance SQLite if you bought them before. The FAQ also answers that series are pre-recorded, videos run 7-10 minutes, it's not an accredited program ("Think of it as a school of thought, not a university"), and student or country-based discounts are available by email.

Fern gives you “Docs, SDKs, and a CLI for your API” from one source of truth—supporting REST, WebSockets, GraphQL, OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, and gRPC—so you can “Upgrade your developer and agent experience.” It’s “Built for the AI era” with docs as code, Ask Fern, llms.txt, an MCP server, AI-assisted authoring, and native Postman support, plus enterprise-ready security, self-hosting, localization, SOC 2 Type II, and support SLAs. No pricing, free tier, or open-source status is shown.

Conductor is a Mac tool for running "a team of coding agents on your Mac." The page itself shows only a status readout — "New cloud workspace," "Building snapshot 0ms ›booting Firecracker microVM ›restoring repository snapshot" — with no pricing, free tier, or open-source details shown.

ui.wiki is Raphael Salaja's publication of essays and code write-ups about interface craft — Animating Container Bounds, Morphing Icons, Generating Sounds with AI, Mastering Animate Presence, Pseudo Elements, To Spring or Not To Spring, 12 Principles of Animation — “There's a set of psychological principles behind every interface that feels right. Here are the ones I think about the most.” Posts run from Apr 8, 2025 to Feb 9, 2026, and no subscription or pricing details appear on the page.

Entire is Git hosting “built for agents, and humans” — “the fastest Git network on Earth,” where agents clone and push up to 89 times faster than the competition, and every commit an agent makes becomes a checkpoint paired with the conversation behind it. Its CLI is open source and MIT licensed, works with any agent, and its semantic graph is “100% local and open source” to cut token spend by up to 71%.

Just fucking use Effect: try-catch is a war crime, Promise.all is a death trap, and your node_modules is a landfill. Effect treats errors as values, gives you retries, timeouts, interruption, cleanup, concurrency, tracing, and OpenTelemetry — it's TypeScript's missing standard library, API stable at v3.0, and built for AI agents with @effect/ai so you can swap OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or Amazon Bedrock without rewriting. And if you're scared of the learning curve, plot twist: LLMs are really fucking good at writing Effect code, so the AI already climbed it for you.

Two kinds of AI users are emerging: the "power users" who are all in on Claude Code, MCPs, skills — surprisingly often not very technical — with finance roles getting enormous value out of a full programming ecosystem, versus "so many people I wouldn't expect" still only chatting to ChatGPT. Enterprise is the bottleneck: locked down environments, legacy software with no internal‑facing APIs, siloed engineering, and M365 Copilot as often the only allowed tool — "a poorly cloned version of the (already not great) ChatGPT interface" — so decision makers write off AI, while smaller companies without the baggage are "absolutely flying." The future is a bash sandbox with a programming language, API access to systems and an agentic harness, and "I don't think there's ever been a time in history where a tiny team can outcompete a company one thousand times its size so easily."

The Books directory lists titles, each with a trail count — "Thinking in Systems" 15 trails, "Seeing Like a State" 11 trails, down to the many that hold a single trail. It points to book pages like Thinking in Systems, Seeing Like a State, Superforecasting, Creativity, Inc., Behave, Zero to One, Chip War, and the rest.

Butter is building bVisor, "an incredibly lightweight sandbox runtime for AI agents." It embeds directly into your local process, providing a safe bash environment without the overhead of VMs or remote infra.

Factory is agent-native software development, built on three pillars: Control — "Sovereign, Model-Independent Intelligence" where you "control where your system runs, how it learns, and which models it uses" — Governance, a "governed system that continuously turns enterprise signals into validated production software," and Value, connecting engineering adoption and effectiveness to "growth, profitability, risk, and business performance."

Devouring Details calls itself "an interactive reference manual for interaction-curious designers, containing 23 chapters with 23 downloadable React components"—not a course: "You won't solve code challenges, answer quizzes, or follow step-by-step tutorials," you'll interact with prototypes on a custom platform and be shown "details that I pay attention to." It's split into 3 units: Principles (Inferring intent, Interaction metaphors, Ergonomic interactions, Simulating physics, Motion choreography, Responsive interfaces, Contained gestures, Drawing inspiration), Prototypes (Line Minimap, Scroll Strip, Radial Timeline, Morph Surface, Line Graph, Logos Carousel, Motion React, Blur Reveal, Time Machine) and Resources ("useful code snippets, insights into my design process, private bookmarks"). Only the Next.js Dev Tools prototype and Behind scenes are marked FREE; everything else's price isn't stated.

Channel3 is "building the world's highest quality product graph, so AI agents can reliably search, recommend, and purchase products," with brand partners like Walmart, Best Buy, and CVS. Because "Discovery is happening inside AI apps and agents," Channel3 "provides the infrastructure to make it happen" — for developers building agentic shopping experiences, brands that want products to appear in AI apps and agents, and enterprises embedding shopping into their platforms.

The Option Method, Bruce Di Marsico's 1970s approach resurfaced via Ari Nielsen and Deborah Mendel, holds that "unhappiness is never necessary — it is always optional": you are unhappy because you believe you must be, and you create that unhappiness yourself for good reasons, which means you can drop it. Emotional beliefs — "I need my partner to appreciate me more to be happy" — are always false, since only your thinking, not circumstance, makes you happy or unhappy; unhappiness is often a distorted signal of something you deeply value, so a Socratic questioning of the belief ("what would I have to believe to feel this way? Is that belief really true?") lets the feeling evaporate even when the situation stays the same. Happiness is your natural state, and the same method works on objections about motivation, hardship, and depression — it isn't spiritual bypass, and it isn't a substitute for professional care.

unavatar is "the universal avatars API: one HTTP endpoint for user profile photos from 75+ sources like GitHub, X, Instagram, and Gravatar" — the same URL pattern also resolves logos, favicons, app icons, and artwork, with "no SDK, no tokens for the free tier, no setup." The free tier covers "25 requests per day per IP with no API key, and 50 requests per day with an API key," and paid usage is "pure pay-as-you-go. No minimums, no commitments" at $0.010 per token, with cached requests "served for free and don't count toward your usage." It's "free, open source, and community-driven" — "inspect the code, open an issue, or contribute a new provider."
This is Sujan Khadgi's site, and the page says only this: "Sujan Khadgi — Product Designer." A title and a name — that's what's here.

Kernel is "browser infrastructure for web agents and automations" — headful or stealth sessions with a CDP websocket URL, captcha clearing, profiles signed in to Google and YouTube, payments filled from an authorized vault, GPU acceleration, EU and APAC regional browsing, and session video replay. It's "loved by 11,000+ teams building agents," with The Prompting Company running 50,000+ Kernel browsers a month and Effective running 10mm+ insurance regulatory filings and 24/7 workloads on it. Per ComputeSDK benchmarks, Kernel does 6.43 actions/sec inside a running session, against Browserbase's 4.00 and browser use's 3.61.

Sam — "Husband, dad, programmer, whisky-drinker, writer" — writes "visual, interactive essays about software," each taking "anywhere from one to three months to create," covering Big O, Reservoir Sampling, Turing Machines, Bloom Filters, Hashing, Memory Allocation and Load Balancing. He does the same kind of writing full-time as a developer educator at ngrok, has been a guest on Hanselminutes and other podcasts, and is on GitHub at samwho with an occasional newsletter at newsletter.samwho.dev.

Smithery is a Model Context Protocol registry where you "Connect agents to thousands of tools and services" — auth, credentials, and sessions handled for you — with 26,056+ MCPs to browse and "Connect once. Use everywhere." Publishers are told "Publish once, install anywhere—with built-in auth and observability," and Smithery Connect is open source, "powered by agent.pw, our open-source agent vault." No sitewide pricing appears on the page; individual servers list their own terms, like DevMatch's "Free tier with 50 monthly credits, $129/mo Pro" or The Local Intel's "$0.01–$0.05/call. Free discovery tier available."

Cold Takes is a run of posts—from “The Most Important Century (in a nutshell)” and “How we could stumble into AI catastrophe” to “Where’s Today’s Beethoven?” and “Cold Links: assorted fun basketball stuff”—dated Jul 13 through Mar 18, with read times from “1 min read” to “25 min read.” The page names no editor or writer, though it speaks in the first person (“Cold Takes reader survey - let me know what you want more and less of!”), and no subscription details are shown.

LessWrong's front page is the post feed — Recent, Enriched, Recommended — and this week it's AI safety and frontier labs: three fired OpenAI safety staffers ("OpenAI fired me last week, along with two of my safety colleagues"), unfixable security vulnerabilities, and CeSIA's "Politicians on AI" tool built from "nearly 200,000 public documents." No editor, masthead, or subscription details appear on the page — just the posts.

Chroma is “Fast, serverless, and scalable infrastructure supporting vector, full-text, regex, and metadata search,” built on object storage, open-source Apache 2.0, and installable with `pip install chromadb` or `npm install chromadb`. Trusted by millions of developers and offering enterprise BYOC, multi-cloud replication, and 0-ops management, it says you can “Get up and running in 30 seconds or less with $5 in free credits,” with Pro and Enterprise plans for support.

GitButler is a free and open source Git client that gives you "Everything You Wished Git Had": stacked branches, parallel branches, unlimited undo/redo, a powerful smartlog, and simple history editing. It's "Built for Coding Agents" — structured JSON output, idempotent commands, and conflict resolution for AI-generated changes — and it "works with any Git repo" with zero configuration required, as its benchmark claims "Agents are 60% faster using GitButler than vanilla Git, with 80% fewer tool calls."

Mediabunny is "a JavaScript library for reading, writing, and converting video and audio files. Directly in the browser, and faster than anybunny else" — 100% TypeScript, zero dependencies, tree-shakable, installed with `npm install mediabunny`. It's "an open-source project released under the MPL-2.0 and is therefore free to use for any purpose, including closed-source commercial use."

Microlink is "APIs and tooling to turn any URL into structured output" — "One REST endpoint for every Microlink product" spanning Screenshot ("Generate pixel-perfect captures for any URL"), Link Preview, Markdown ("Built for agents handling website content"), Metadata, Embed, Search, PDF ("Create production-ready PDFs from live webpages"), Text ("Extract clean, LLM-ready text from any page") and more. It also points to tools built on top of the Microlink API, like Editor, Website Screenshot, URL to Markdown, Bulk Screenshots and Bulk URLs to PDFs.

Real-world case studies from Vio, DoorDash, Preply, GeekyAnts, and Inngest show teams pushing advanced React and Next.js techniques into production — profiling INP, migrating from CSR to SSR, adopting RSC and the App Router — with results like DoorDash's LCP dropping 65% and Preply's INP falling under the 200ms "good" threshold. The distilled takeaways: optimize Core Web Vitals methodically, "reduce code on the client to a minimum," strike a balance between SSR and CSR, cache deliberately, and keep state management simple — "simpler is often better."

Microlink Geolocation gives you "IP-based location data, simplified" — "detailed information about the incoming request based on the IP address," returned as JSON from "just one HTTP request." It's "Free" with "No API key needed," and you can view it on GitHub.

metascraper is "a library to easily extract unified metadata from websites using Open Graph, Microdata, RDFa, Twitter Cards, JSON-LD, HTML, and more": give it the target URL and the HTML markup, and it returns author, date, title, image, logo, publisher and other fields. It's "a collection of tiny packages, so you can just use what you actually need," and it's built out of rules bundles that work as fallbacks for one another, from most specific to most generic. Running this at scale means "operating headless browsers, proxies, and antibot workarounds" — if you don't want to manage that infrastructure, the fully managed Microlink API is pay-as-you-go and "starts for free."

Ye Olde Blogroll is a manually curated directory of personal sites — "Because blogs are the soul of the web." Its 100 entries point outward to personal blogs, digital gardens and old-fashioned diaries, from a "polymath who loves the smell of freshly baked thoughts (and bread) in the morning" to someone whose "blog is like a box of chocolates."

Tolan is an "Alien Best Friend": friendly guides built on top of the leading AI models, where the real work is in "the complex systems that shape how a Tolan listens, responds, remembers, and knows when to step back" — an experience that feels "genuinely warm, fun, and natural without pretending to be human." It has 250,000+ active users, over 8 million hours spent with Tolan guides, and a 4.8-star App Store rating across 180,000+ reviews; in a user survey, 85.6% said their Tolan helped them get through an emotionally difficult experience and 72.5% said it helped them manage or improve a relationship. The team is backed by $30M+ in capital and is hiring in San Francisco for "embodied AI that puts people first."

Beautifully crafted animated icons* — an open-source (MIT License) collection of smooth animated icons for your projects. Crafted with Motion & Lucide and installable via `pnpm dlx shadcn add @lucide-animated/`: "feel free to use them, share your feedback, and let's make this library awesome together."

Pika is an online screenshot beautifier and mockup generator: capture from a URL or the Chrome extension, then add frames, backgrounds and annotations — "Capture. Customize. Save." — and export high-quality images sized for social media, docs, landing pages and app stores. It's free without an account for unlimited exports with a small "designed in Pika.style" watermark, while Pika Pro ($15 a month or $150 a year, plus a $299 lifetime plan and a $12-per-seat Team plan) adds text, annotations, custom canvas sizes, 4K, SVG and WebP export, share links and saved presets.

Udara Jay's page is a shelf of writing — making a world, proactive AI, virtual cells, embeddings, bioinformatics, homelab, design engineering — alongside open-source work: Tiny router, "a compact multi-head routing classifier," Pile, a reflective journaling app, and Stats, a self-hosted analytics provider.
